crit: The cattle|Methane from digestion and the land cleared for pasture and feed are most of the footprint. Nothing done after the farm comes close.
look: Where it was raised|Beef from recently deforested regions carries the largest carbon and wildlife cost. Country and region of origin is the most useful thing on the label.
Organic or pasture-raised certification|Independently checked rules on feed, antibiotics and outdoor access. Better for welfare and local wildlife, not lower in methane.
Smaller portion, less often|No label changes beef's footprint as much as eating less of it.
beware: 'Carbon-neutral beef'|Usually relies on offsets or soil-carbon estimates that are hard to verify.
'Natural' or 'farm fresh'|Not regulated terms and say nothing about how the animal was raised.

crit: Feed crops|Soy and maize for feed are most of the footprint, and soy is linked to forest clearance in South America.
Antibiotic use|Routine dosing in crowded sheds drives drug-resistant bacteria.
look: Organic|Requires outdoor access, slower-growing birds and bans routine antibiotics.
Free-range or a recognised higher-welfare scheme|For example RSPCA Assured, Better Chicken Commitment, Label Rouge or Animal Welfare Approved.
'Raised without antibiotics' with a certifier named|Meaningful when a third party audits it.
beware: 'Farm fresh', 'natural', 'corn-fed'|Describe marketing or diet, not welfare or environmental standards.
'Hormone-free'|Hormones are already banned in poultry in most countries, so the claim tells you nothing.

crit: How and where it was caught or farmed|The species, the fishing gear and the stock's health decide almost everything. Bottom trawling and overfished stocks are the worst cases.
look: MSC blue label|Wild fish from a fishery independently assessed as sustainable.
ASC label|Farmed fish and shellfish meeting audited environmental and social standards.
Species and catch method on the pack|Pole-and-line, handline and pot-caught are low-damage. A seafood guide such as Seafood Watch or the Good Fish Guide rates each species.
Mussels, oysters, sardines, mackerel|Naturally low-impact choices whatever the label.
beware: 'Responsibly sourced' with no certifier|An unverified company claim.
'Dolphin safe'|Covers one bycatch issue for tuna and says nothing about the health of the stock.

crit: Growing the beans|Farming is the hotspot: forest cleared for sun-grown coffee, and farmers who are often paid less than it costs to produce.
The milk|In a latte, milk is often more of the carbon than the coffee.
look: Fairtrade|Guarantees a minimum price and a premium to farmer cooperatives.
Rainforest Alliance (frog seal)|Audited standards on forest protection, farming practice and worker rights.
Organic|No synthetic pesticides or fertiliser.
Smithsonian Bird Friendly|The strictest shade-grown standard: coffee grown under forest canopy.
Named farm or cooperative and a published price|Direct-trade roasters that say who they paid and how much.
beware: 'Ethically sourced' with no certifier|Means whatever the brand wants it to mean.
'Compostable' pods and cups|Usually only break down in industrial composting, which most places do not collect for.

crit: Plantation labour|Tea is picked by hand, and estate workers in Assam, Kenya and Sri Lanka are among the lowest paid in farming.
Boiling the water|Most of a cup's carbon is the kettle.
look: Fairtrade|Minimum price plus a premium that workers decide how to spend.
Rainforest Alliance|Audited environmental and labour standards on estates.
Ethical Tea Partnership membership|Industry programme on wages and conditions.
Organic, loose leaf|No synthetic pesticides and no plastic in the bag.
beware: 'Plastic-free' tea bags|Many are bio-plastic (PLA) that needs industrial composting.
'Natural'|Unregulated.

crit: How it travelled|Shipped fruit is low-carbon. Air-freighted berries, mangoes and out-of-season exotics can be ten times higher.
Pesticides and plantation labour|The main issue for bananas, pineapples and grapes.
look: Country of origin and season|Local and in season is the safest rule; far away and highly perishable usually means it flew.
Fairtrade (bananas, pineapples, citrus)|Better pay and pesticide protections for plantation workers.
Organic|No synthetic pesticides.
Rainforest Alliance|Common on bananas; covers environmental and labour practice.
Loose, unwrapped, slightly imperfect|Less packaging and less waste.
beware: 'By air' stickers are rare|Most air-freighted produce is not labelled as such, so origin plus perishability is your clue.

crit: Heated greenhouses|Out-of-season tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers grown under heat can emit ten times more than field-grown.
Waste at home|Vegetables are the most thrown-away food.
look: Season and origin|Field-grown, in season, from your region.
Organic|No synthetic pesticides or fertiliser; better for soil life and insects.
LEAF Marque, GlobalG.A.P. or similar farm assurance|Audited farming standards.
Loose rather than pre-packed|Buy the amount you will eat.
beware: 'Locally grown' in winter|May mean a heated greenhouse, which can be worse than produce shipped from somewhere sunny.

crit: Nitrogen fertiliser on the wheat|About 40% of a loaf's footprint, and a major river pollutant.
Waste|Bread is one of the most binned foods.
look: Organic|No synthetic nitrogen fertiliser.
Wholegrain as the first ingredient|Better for you and uses more of the grain.
Short ingredient list|Flour, water, salt, yeast. Long lists mark ultra-processed bread.
A local bakery, or regenerative-farming flour with a named standard|Shorter chain, and you can ask.
beware: 'Multigrain' or 'brown'|Can still be mostly refined white flour with colouring.
'Baked in store'|Often part-baked elsewhere and finished on site.

crit: The cheese and any meat|Dairy and meat toppings are most of the footprint; the base is minor.
look: Vegetable toppings|The biggest single reduction.
Organic or higher-welfare dairy and meat|Where the pack or menu says so.
Eco-Score or similar front-of-pack rating|On frozen pizzas in some countries.
Recyclable cardboard without a plastic window|For frozen and takeaway boxes.
beware: 'Plant-based' on a cheese-heavy pizza|Check what it actually refers to.

crit: The cows|Methane, feed and slurry. It takes roughly ten litres of milk to make a kilo of cheese.
look: Organic|Pasture access, no routine antibiotics, no synthetic fertiliser on feed.
Pasture-fed or free-range dairy schemes|For example Pasture for Life or grass-fed certifications with an auditor.
Animal-welfare certification|RSPCA Assured, Certified Humane, Beter Leven or equivalent.
Plant-based alternative with added calcium|Oat and soy have the lowest overall footprints.
beware: 'Farm fresh' and pictures of meadows|Most dairy cows in intensive systems spend much or all of the year indoors.
'Carbon-neutral milk'|Usually offset-based.

crit: Cocoa farming in West Africa|The hotspot for both people and forests: child labour, farmer poverty and forest clearance are concentrated here.
Palm oil and milk|Secondary hotspots in filled and milk chocolate.
look: Fairtrade|Minimum price and premium for cocoa cooperatives.
Rainforest Alliance|Audited farm standards; the most common cocoa label.
Brands that publish their farms and what they paid|Full traceability and a living-income price go further than certification. Independent rankings such as the Chocolate Scorecard compare brands.
Organic|No synthetic pesticides.
RSPO-certified or no palm oil|For filled bars and spreads.
beware: Company-own schemes|Programmes named after the brand are self-assessed; look for independent audits.
'Sustainably sourced cocoa' with no detail|Often 'mass balance': certified and uncertified beans are mixed.

crit: The hen's housing and feed|Welfare is decided by the system: cage, barn, free-range or organic. Feed is the environmental hotspot.
look: The code stamped on the egg (EU/UK)|0 organic, 1 free-range, 2 barn, 3 caged.
Organic|Most space, outdoor access, organic feed.
Free-range or pasture-raised with a certifier|Certified Humane, RSPCA Assured, Animal Welfare Approved.
Local, with a named farm|Easy to check.
beware: 'Farm fresh', 'natural', 'vegetarian-fed'|Say nothing about how the hens live.
'Cage-free' (US)|Indoors in a barn, not outdoors.

crit: The bottle|For wine and spirits, glass is often the largest part of the footprint.
Your health|No level of drinking is risk-free.
look: Lightweight bottle, can, keg or box|A bag-in-box wine has roughly a tenth of the packaging footprint of glass.
Organic or biodynamic (Demeter)|No synthetic pesticides in vineyards and hop fields.
Local brewery or refill scheme|Short transport and reused containers.
B Corp or published footprint|Some producers report and reduce their emissions.
beware: Heavy 'premium' bottles|Weight signals luxury and adds nothing to the drink.
'Natural wine'|No legal definition.

crit: The aluminium can and the sugar|Smelting new aluminium is extremely energy-hungry; the sugar is the health and water issue.
look: Recycling mark and a deposit scheme|An aluminium can recycles endlessly if it gets back.
Sugar per 100 ml on the nutrition panel|Under 5 g is low; many soft drinks are near 10 g.
Nutri-Score or traffic-light label|Quick health read where used.
Recycled-content claim with a percentage|Some cans state it.
beware: 'Zero' and 'diet'|Remove the sugar, not the can or the chilled supply chain.
'100% recyclable'|True of almost every can and bottle; what matters is whether it is recycled where you live.

crit: The single-use plastic bottle itself|Made from oil and gas, used for minutes, and usually not recycled into a new bottle.
look: A tap|In most cities tap water is tested more often than bottled.
Refill points and a durable bottle|Stainless steel or glass, used for years.
100% recycled PET (rPET) stated on the bottle|If you must buy one.
A deposit-return scheme|Raises collection rates to around 90%.
beware: 'Plant-based' or 'biodegradable' bottles|Still plastic, still litter, and can contaminate recycling.
'Ocean-bound plastic'|A loosely defined term with no single standard.

crit: The animal products on the plate|Whether a meal contains beef, lamb or a lot of cheese changes its footprint more than anything else.
What is left over|A third of food is never eaten.
look: Plant-forward dishes|The single most reliable choice.
Eco-Score, carbon labels or menu footprints|Appearing on packs and some menus.
Organic, Fairtrade, MSC or free-range on the main ingredients|The label on the highest-impact ingredient matters most.
A portion you will finish|Or a box to take the rest home.
beware: 'Local' on a meat dish|How it was produced matters far more than how far it travelled.

crit: Cotton growing|The thirstiest and most pesticide-heavy stage, often in water-stressed regions.
Wet processing|Dyeing and finishing are where the worst water pollution and much of the energy use happen.
look: GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard)|The strongest label: organic fibre plus audited chemical, water and labour rules through the whole chain.
Fairtrade Cotton|Minimum price and premium for cotton farmers.
OEKO-TEX Standard 100, or Made in Green|Tested for harmful substances; Made in Green adds audited factories.
bluesign|Controls chemicals and water at the dye house.
Fair Wear Foundation membership|The brand is independently checked on factory labour conditions.
Second-hand|No label beats a garment that already exists.
beware: 'Conscious', 'eco', 'sustainable collection'|Brand-invented ranges with no standard behind them.
'Made with organic cotton'|May be a small percentage; look for the share and a certifier.
'Recycled polyester'|Usually from bottles, not old clothes, and still sheds microfibres.

crit: Cotton, then the fabric mill|Two-thirds of the water is in growing the cotton; dyeing and finishing denim is the main pollution and energy hotspot.
Finishing|Sandblasting and chemical 'distressing' have harmed workers' lungs.
look: GOTS or organic cotton with a percentage|Certified fibre and processing.
Raw or rinse-wash denim|Skips the most water- and chemical-intensive finishing.
EU Ecolabel or bluesign|Audited limits on chemicals and water in production.
Repair or lifetime-guarantee programme|Brands that fix their jeans expect them to last.
Second-hand or vintage|Denim is the easiest garment to buy used.
beware: 'Waterless' denim|Often refers to one finishing step, not the cotton, where most water is used.
Pre-ripped styles|More processing and a shorter life.

crit: Manufacturing|Moulding, stitching and gluing some 65 parts in factories mostly run on coal power. Glued construction also makes shoes unrecyclable.
Leather tanning|Where leather is used, chrome tanning is the pollution hotspot.
look: Stitched, resoleable construction|A shoe a cobbler can repair lasts years longer.
Leather Working Group (Gold or Silver)|Audits tanneries for water, energy and chemical management.
Fair Wear, Fair Labor Association or published factory list|Evidence the brand checks working conditions.
Repair or take-back service|Run by the brand or a local cobbler.
Recycled or natural rubber with FSC certification|For soles.
beware: 'Vegan leather'|Usually polyurethane or PVC: plastic with a shorter life.
'Made with recycled materials'|Often one small component.
'Carbon neutral' shoes|Offset claims; ask what was actually reduced.

crit: The tannery|For leather, tanning with chromium salts is the main pollution and worker-health hotspot.
Cattle supply|Hides from deforested land carry that footprint with them.
look: Leather Working Group rating|Tannery audited for chemicals, water and traceability.
Vegetable-tanned leather|Avoids chromium.
Traceable hide origin|Brands that name the tannery and the country the hides came from.
Repair service and solid stitching|A bag built to be fixed.
Second-hand|A large resale market exists.
beware: 'Genuine leather'|A grade, and a low one, not a mark of quality or ethics.
'Vegan leather'|Usually plastic.
'Eco-leather'|No agreed meaning.

crit: The mine|Gold and gemstone mining is the hotspot: tonnes of waste rock per ring, cyanide and mercury pollution, and dangerous labour in small-scale mines.
look: Recycled gold or silver, with a certifier|For example Responsible Jewellery Council Chain-of-Custody or SCS Recycled Content.
Fairmined or Fairtrade Gold|Traceable to small-scale mines with mercury controls and fair pay.
Lab-grown stones|No mining.
Kimberley Process plus a named mine of origin|The Kimberley Process alone only screens for conflict financing, so origin detail matters.
Vintage, antique or remodelled pieces|The metal is already above ground.
beware: 'Conflict-free'|Narrowly defined; does not cover labour abuse or environmental damage.
'Ethically sourced' with no chain of custody|Unverifiable.
'Eco-friendly gold'|Not a standard.

crit: The battery minerals|Cobalt and lithium: most cobalt comes from the DR Congo, where child labour in small mines is documented.
Chip and screen manufacturing|Where about 80% of the carbon and most of the water is used.
look: Repairability score|France's index, the EU energy label's repair class or an iFixit score. Seven out of ten or better is good.
Years of software updates promised|Five or more means the phone can actually last.
Refurbished with a warranty|Roughly 80–90% lower footprint than new.
EPEAT or TCO Certified|Independent standards covering materials, energy, labour and end of life.
Replaceable battery and spare parts on sale|The EU will require user-replaceable batteries from 2027.
Fairtrade gold, recycled cobalt or a published supplier list|Evidence of mineral due diligence.
beware: 'Carbon neutral' devices|Rely on offsets; look at reported manufacturing emissions instead.
'Recycled materials' with no percentage|Often a tiny share by weight.
Trade-in deals that push yearly upgrades|The greenest phone is the one you already have.

crit: Chips, board and display|75–85% of the footprint is manufacturing, concentrated in semiconductors.
Battery and solder metals|Cobalt, tin, tantalum and gold carry the mining risks.
look: TCO Certified|The most demanding IT label: covers factory labour, hazardous substances, repairability and lifespan.
EPEAT Gold|Life-cycle environmental standard.
Energy Star or EU energy label|Efficiency in use.
Repairability: upgradeable memory and storage, replaceable battery|Check the manual or an iFixit score.
Refurbished business-grade model with warranty|Built to last and far lower footprint.
beware: Soldered memory and glued batteries|Thin designs that cannot be upgraded or repaired.
'Made with ocean plastic'|Usually a small part of the casing.

crit: The panel factory|Display manufacturing uses large amounts of energy and fluorinated gases thousands of times stronger than CO₂.
Electricity over its life|Roughly half the footprint, and it rises steeply with screen size.
look: Energy label|EU A–G scale or Energy Star: compare kWh per 1,000 hours.
A size that fits the room|Each size up adds both manufacturing and running impact.
EPEAT or TCO Certified|Where available for displays.
Spare parts and repair availability|EU rules require parts for at least seven years.
Refurbished or ex-display|Avoids a new panel.
beware: 'Eco mode' as a selling point|Often switched off by default or by the user because it dims the picture.
8K|Much higher energy use for a difference most people cannot see.

crit: The sealed battery|Glued-in cells that cannot be replaced are why most wireless earbuds are thrown away within a few years.
look: Replaceable battery, pads and cable|Or a wired model, which has no battery to fail.
Spare parts sold by the maker|And an iFixit or repairability score.
Recycled plastics with a stated percentage|Some makers publish it.
Take-back or trade-in scheme|And a proper e-waste collection point at end of life.
Volume-limiting feature|Protects your hearing.
beware: 'Recyclable'|Technically true, rarely done for small mixed electronics.
Cheap disposable-grade earbuds|Lowest price, shortest life.

crit: Where the wood came from|Legal, well-managed forest versus illegal logging is the biggest difference between two similar pieces.
Glues, foams and finishes|Particleboard resins and flame-retardant foams are the health and recycling problem.
look: FSC (ideally FSC 100%)|The most credible forest certification.
PEFC|Widely used alternative forest certification.
Solid wood with screwed or jointed construction|Can be repaired and refinished.
Low-emission marks|GREENGUARD Gold, EU Ecolabel, Blue Angel, or E1/E0 board for formaldehyde.
Second-hand, antique or refurbished|No new material at all.
Spare parts and a long guarantee|Signs it was built to last.
beware: 'FSC Mix'|Legitimate, but may contain as little as 70% certified or recycled fibre.
'Eco-friendly' or 'sustainable wood' with no certificate|Unverified.
Bamboo as automatically green|Depends on glue, processing and shipping.

crit: Pulp and paper making|The energy- and water-intensive step, and where the forest source matters.
look: FSC or PEFC logo on the imprint page|Paper from certified or recycled sources.
Recycled-paper content|Stated by some publishers.
Vegetable-based inks, Cradle to Cradle or Blue Angel|For low-toxicity printing.
A library card or second-hand copy|Shared reading is the lowest-impact reading.
beware: 'Tree-free' or 'stone paper'|Often plastic-bound and not recyclable with paper.

crit: The electricity it uses|Almost the whole footprint, so efficiency and your power source decide it.
Light spilling into the night|The main harm to wildlife.
look: Lumens per watt on the energy label|Over 100 lm/W is efficient; the EU label runs A to G.
Warm colour temperature for evenings and outdoors|2,700 K or lower disturbs sleep and insects least.
Replaceable bulb, not a sealed fixture|So a failed LED does not scrap the lamp.
Fully shielded outdoor fittings, DarkSky Approved|Light goes down, not up.
A renewable electricity tariff|Changes the footprint of everything you plug in.
beware: 'Integrated LED' fittings|When the light source fails the whole lamp is waste.
Very cheap unbranded LEDs|Often fail early and flicker.

crit: How many times it is used|A reusable only beats disposables after tens of uses. The kiln firing and your hot water are the rest.
look: Durable, plain, dishwasher-safe|It only works if you keep using it.
Lead- and cadmium-free glaze|Stated by reputable makers; matters for vintage and imported ceramics.
Second-hand|Charity shops are full of them.
Local pottery|Short supply chain and repairable relationships.
beware: Bamboo-fibre 'eco' cups|Usually bound with melamine resin, not recyclable, and can leach with hot drinks.
Buying a new reusable for every occasion|Defeats the purpose.

crit: What happens after you finish with it|Minutes of use, centuries of persistence. Only about 9% of plastic ever made has been recycled.
look: No packaging, or refill|Avoiding it beats recycling it.
Resin code 1 (PET) or 2 (HDPE)|The plastics with real recycling markets. Films and mixed materials mostly are not recycled.
Mono-material packaging|One plastic type is recyclable; laminated layers are not.
Recycled content with a percentage|Shows demand for collected plastic.
Certified home-compostable (OK compost HOME, AS 5810)|The only compostable claim that works without industrial facilities.
beware: 'Biodegradable' or 'oxo-degradable'|Often just fragments into microplastic; oxo-degradables are banned in the EU.
The chasing-arrows triangle|Identifies the plastic type; it does not mean it will be recycled.
'Compostable' without a home-compost certificate|Needs industrial composting that most places lack.

crit: Plastic and a short life|About 90% of toys are plastic, used briefly and almost never recycled.
Chemicals|Softeners and paints are the safety concern in cheap or old plastic toys.
look: Safety marks|CE or UKCA in Europe, ASTM F963 in the US.
FSC-certified wood|For wooden toys.
Sturdy, repairable, no built-in battery|Toys that survive several children.
Toy libraries, swaps and second-hand|The lowest-impact toy is a shared one.
Ethical Toy Program or Fair Toys Organisation|Factory labour audits.
beware: 'Eco plastic' or 'bioplastic' toys|Still not recyclable in practice.
Toys with sealed batteries and electronics|Become e-waste.

crit: The product itself|Tobacco kills up to half of its long-term users. The filter is a plastic that leaches toxins as litter.
look: Stop-smoking support|Counselling plus nicotine replacement roughly triples the chance of quitting.
A pocket ashtray and a bin|Butts are the most littered item on Earth.
Collection points for vapes|They contain lithium batteries and must not go in general waste.
beware: 'Light', 'mild', 'organic' or 'additive-free' tobacco|None is safer; several of these terms are banned as misleading.
'Biodegradable' filters|Still toxic litter.
Tobacco-industry sustainability awards|Do not change what the product does.

crit: Electricity over its life|Most of the footprint for anything that runs daily.
The refrigerant|In fridges, freezers, air conditioners and heat pumps, leaked gas can outweigh years of electricity.
look: Energy label|EU A–G, Energy Star, or your country's star rating; compare kWh per year, not just the letter.
Natural refrigerant: R290 (propane) or R600a (isobutane)|Hundreds of times less warming than older HFC gases.
Spare parts and repair information|EU rules require parts for seven to ten years; a repairability score helps.
The right size|An oversized fridge or air conditioner wastes energy every day.
Certified take-back on delivery|So the old unit is degassed properly.
beware: 'Eco' programme labels|Check the measured kWh and water figures instead.
Smart features as an efficiency claim|Connectivity itself uses standby power.
Replacing a working appliance to save energy|Rarely pays back the footprint of making the new one.

crit: Heating the water|The carbon is in the hot water, not the water itself.
Your local source|How scarce water is where you live decides how much each litre matters.
look: Flow rate on showers and taps|8 litres a minute or less for a shower. Labels: Unified Water Label (Europe), WaterSense (US), WELS (Australia).
Dual-flush or low-flush toilet|4/2.6 litres per flush or better.
How your water is heated|Heat pump or solar hot water cuts the carbon most.
Your water utility's source and quality report|Tells you which river or aquifer you depend on.
beware: 'Eco' shower heads without a flow figure|The number is what matters.
Flushable wipes|Do not break down; they block sewers.

crit: Palm-oil derivatives and mica|Palm derivatives hide under hundreds of ingredient names; mica for shimmer is linked to child labour.
What washes down the drain|UV filters, microplastics and persistent chemicals.
look: COSMOS or NATRUE|Audited natural and organic cosmetics standards.
EU Ecolabel, Nordic Swan or Blue Angel|Life-cycle ecolabels with strict limits on harmful chemicals.
Leaping Bunny|The most rigorous cruelty-free certification.
RSPO certified palm oil|Segregated or identity-preserved is strongest.
Refill, solid bar or concentrated formats|Less packaging and less water shipped.
Responsible Mica Initiative membership|For make-up with shimmer.
beware: 'Clean', 'natural', 'non-toxic', 'dermatologist tested'|Unregulated marketing terms.
'Reef-safe'|No legal definition; check for non-nano zinc oxide instead.
'Free from' lists|Often advertise the absence of things that were never used.

crit: Synthetic materials|Most gear is plastic, rubber or foam made from oil. For clothing, PFAS waterproofing is the chemical to watch.
look: Repair and spare-parts service|From the brand or a local shop.
PFC-free or PFAS-free water repellent|Now offered by most outdoor brands.
bluesign or OEKO-TEX|For sportswear fabrics.
Fair Wear or Fair Labor Association|Factory labour monitoring.
Rent, borrow or buy used|Especially for gear you use a few times a year.
beware: 'Recycled ocean plastic' kit|Usually a small share, and it still sheds microfibres.
New gear for every new activity|Try it first.

crit: Where the institution lends and invests|Your deposit or pension is put to work. Fossil-fuel expansion and deforestation-linked companies are the hotspots.
look: A published fossil-fuel exclusion policy|Clear, dated limits on financing new oil, gas and coal.
Independent bank rankings|Banking on Climate Chaos, Fair Finance Guide, bank.green or Ethical Consumer.
Pension fund defaults and voting record|Ask which fund you are in and how it votes on climate resolutions.
B Corp, Global Alliance for Banking on Values|Banks built around social and environmental lending.
Fund labels with standards behind them|EU SFDR Article 9, Nordic Swan, FNG Siegel, Towards Sustainability.
beware: 'ESG' or 'sustainable' fund names|Many hold oil majors; check the top ten holdings.
'Net zero by 2050' pledges|Look for what the bank is financing this year.
Trees planted per card payment|Marketing that says nothing about the loan book.

crit: Burning the fuel|The exhaust over the car's life dwarfs everything else for petrol and diesel.
Battery minerals|For electric cars, lithium, nickel and cobalt mining is the issue to watch.
Size and weight|Heavier cars need more of everything, including tyres and road space.
look: Official CO₂ in g/km and fuel or energy use|On the EU energy label, window sticker or fuel-economy label.
Green NCAP stars|Independent rating of real-world emissions and efficiency.
The smallest car that does the job|Weight matters for every fuel type.
For EVs: battery passport, recycled content and warranty|EU battery passports start in 2027.
Low-rolling-resistance, low-wear tyres|The EU tyre label rates efficiency, grip and noise.
Car-share membership|Each shared car replaces several owned ones.
beware: 'Self-charging hybrid'|Runs on petrol; only plug-ins and full EVs use grid electricity.
Plug-in hybrids that are never plugged in|Real-world emissions are often several times the official figure.
'Zero emissions'|True at the tailpipe only.

crit: The frame and, on e-bikes, the battery|Aluminium, carbon fibre and lithium cells carry most of the manufacturing footprint. It is repaid by riding.
look: Standard, replaceable parts|Common bottom bracket, wheel and brake sizes keep a bike on the road for decades.
A steel or aluminium frame over carbon fibre|Repairable and recyclable.
For e-bikes: battery safety certification (UL 2849 or EN 15194) and a replaceable, brand-supported battery|Safety and lifespan.
Second-hand or refurbished from a bike co-op|Good bikes last 30 years.
A local shop that services what it sells|Maintenance is what keeps you riding.
beware: Very cheap 'bike-shaped objects'|Non-standard parts that cannot be serviced.
Uncertified e-bike batteries and chargers|A real fire risk.

crit: Exhaust and noise|Small engines often lack the emission controls of cars.
Rider safety|The largest impact is on the person riding it.
look: Euro 5 (or the current local) emissions standard|Far cleaner than older models.
Electric models with a certified, swappable battery|No exhaust, low running cost.
Helmet certification|ECE 22.06, DOT or Snell.
ABS brakes|Cut fatal crashes by about a third.
beware: Two-stroke engines|Much higher pollution.
Removing the exhaust baffles or catalytic converter|More noise and pollution, and usually illegal.

crit: How full it is and what powers it|An electric train or a well-used bus is very low-carbon per passenger.
look: Electric or hydrogen fleet markings|Many operators label zero-emission vehicles.
A season pass or integrated ticket|Makes it the default choice.
Operator sustainability or punctuality reports|Public bodies publish them.
Bike parking and step-free access|Signs of a system designed for everyone.
beware: 'Carbon neutral' operators relying on offsets|Check what the vehicles actually run on.

crit: Jet fuel burned at altitude|CO₂ plus contrails and nitrogen oxides, which roughly double the warming. There is no scalable clean substitute yet.
look: Direct flights in economy|Take-off burns the most fuel, and premium seats take several times the space.
Newer, more efficient aircraft|Flight search tools show estimated emissions per seat.
A rail alternative|For trips under about 700 km.
Airline reporting to CDP or SBTi-validated targets|Evidence of real reduction plans.
beware: Carbon offsets at checkout|Many forest offsets have been shown to overstate their benefit several times over.
'Sustainable aviation fuel' flights|SAF is well under 1% of jet fuel; a single flight's claim is an accounting allocation.
'Net zero' airlines|No airline has a demonstrated path yet.

crit: Its age and roots|Big, old trees do most of the work and cannot be replaced in a lifetime. Soil compaction and root damage are what kill urban trees.
look: Native species for your area|Support many times more wildlife than exotic ones.
Local tree-protection rules|Many places protect mature trees; check before any work.
A certified arborist|ISA, Arboricultural Association or equivalent for pruning and health checks.
Locally grown, peat-free nursery stock|Avoids imported pests and diseases.
Community tree groups|Planting and aftercare, which matters more than planting.
beware: 'A tree planted for every purchase'|Ask who plants it, what species, where, and how many survive five years.
Topping or heavy pruning|Shortens a tree's life.

crit: The compost and the nursery|Peat extraction destroys carbon-rich bogs; heated greenhouses and long transport are the rest.
look: Peat-free on the bag or pot|The single most important label in gardening.
Grown in your country or region|Fewer transport miles and less risk of imported pests.
Organic or pesticide-free plants|Many 'bee-friendly' plants are sold pre-treated with insecticides.
Native wildflowers and single (not double) flowers|Accessible nectar and pollen.
Pots that are recycled, recyclable or returned|Black plastic pots are often not sorted by recycling plants.
Fairtrade or Fair Flowers Fair Plants cut flowers|For bouquets.
beware: 'Reduced peat'|Still peat.
'Bee-friendly' logos with no pesticide statement|Ask whether neonicotinoids were used.
Air-purifying plant claims|The effect in a real room is negligible.

crit: The meat in its food|Almost all of a dog's footprint. Flea and tick chemicals are the other issue, for rivers.
look: Complete food made from by-products, insect protein or lower-carbon meats|Meets nutritional standards (FEDIAF or AAFCO) with a smaller footprint.
MSC-certified fish ingredients|Where fish is used.
Vet advice on whether year-round flea treatment is needed|Oral or as-needed treatment keeps insecticide out of water.
Certified compostable waste bags, binned|Not left on the path.
A rescue or a breeder who health-tests|Adoption first.
beware: 'Human-grade' premium meat diets|The highest footprint of all.
'Biodegradable' poo bags left in nature|They do not break down outdoors.
'Grain-free' as a health claim|Not shown to benefit most dogs.

crit: Hunting|Outdoor cats are a leading human-linked cause of bird and small-mammal deaths.
Meat-based food and clay litter|The carbon and mining footprint.
look: Indoor time at dawn and dusk, or a catio|The most effective wildlife protection.
Bright collar cover with a quick-release clasp|Roughly halves bird catches.
Plant-based litter|Wood, paper, corn or wheat rather than strip-mined bentonite clay.
Food using by-products, with MSC fish|Lower footprint, complete nutrition (FEDIAF or AAFCO).
Neutering and adoption|Prevents stray populations.
beware: 'Flushable' litter|Cat waste carries a parasite harmful to marine mammals; do not flush it.
Bells alone|Less effective than bright collar covers.

crit: Insects and habitat|Almost all land birds feed insects to their chicks. Pesticides, tidy gardens, glass and cats are the pressures.
look: Native plants, berries and seed heads left over winter|Food and shelter.
Window markers spaced about 5 cm apart|Prevent collisions.
Clean feeders and fresh water|Dirty feeders spread disease.
Bird-friendly coffee and wildlife-friendly farm labels|Smithsonian Bird Friendly, organic, Fair to Nature.
Citizen-science counts|eBird, the Big Garden Birdwatch, Christmas Bird Count.
beware: Feeding bread|Poor nutrition.
Rodenticides|Poison owls and hawks that eat the rodents.

crit: Flowers and nesting places|Loss of flower-rich habitat is the main cause of decline, followed by insecticides, especially neonicotinoids.
look: Organic food and plants|No synthetic insecticides.
Native wildflower seed from a local source|Matched to local insects.
Plants sold as grown without neonicotinoids|Ask the nursery directly.
Farm labels that require habitat|Bee Better Certified, Fair to Nature, LEAF Marque, Demeter.
A patch left unmown and stems left standing|Most wild bees nest in soil or hollow stems.
beware: Honeybee hives as conservation|Honeybees are livestock and can outcompete wild bees.
Bee hotels that are never cleaned|Can spread parasites; natural stems and bare soil are better.
'Save the bees' products|Check what they actually fund.

crit: The few big choices|Travel, diet, home energy and where your money sits make up most of a typical footprint. Small habits matter far less.
look: A footprint calculator based on national data|Shows your own biggest category in ten minutes.
Your electricity and heating source|Often the easiest large switch.
Your bank and pension|Covered under Money.
Your workplace and local council|Where one voice can change many footprints.
Credible labels on big purchases|Energy labels, repairability scores, FSC, Fairtrade, organic.
beware: Feeling it all rests on you|Systems set most of the options; your vote and voice count as actions.
Offsets as a way to carry on unchanged|Reduce first.

crit: Methane and land|Digestion in cattle and sheep, and the pasture and feed land they need, are the dominant impacts.
look: Organic or pasture-based certification|Pasture for Life, Organic, Animal Welfare Approved.
Low stocking density and mixed farming|Grazing that maintains meadows and hedgerows.
Named farm and breed|Traceability you can check.
Higher-welfare labels|RSPCA Assured, Certified Humane, Beter Leven.
beware: 'Regenerative' without a standard|A promising idea with no single definition; ask what is measured.
Claims that grazing cancels the methane|Soil carbon gains are real but limited and level off.

crit: Heating and cooling|The largest running impact of most homes.
Cement and steel|The 'embodied carbon' emitted before anyone moves in.
look: Energy performance rating|EPC (Europe), HERS or Energy Star (US), NABERS or NatHERS (Australia).
Insulation and airtightness first, then a heat pump|In that order.
Green building certifications|Passivhaus, LEED, BREEAM, DGNB, Living Building Challenge.
Environmental Product Declarations and low-carbon concrete|For new builds and renovations.
FSC timber and low-VOC paints|Healthier indoors.
Renovating rather than demolishing|The existing structure has already paid its carbon.
beware: 'Eco-home' marketing without a rating|Ask for the certificate.
Gas boilers sold as 'hydrogen-ready'|Hydrogen for home heating is unlikely to arrive at scale.
'Net zero' buildings relying on offsets|Check actual energy use.

crit: Polysilicon production|Energy-intensive and concentrated in a region with documented forced-labour concerns, so supply-chain traceability is the thing to ask about.
look: Supply-chain traceability statement|Makers that publish where their polysilicon comes from; the Solar Stewardship Initiative certifies this.
Product and performance warranty of 25 years or more|A sign of quality.
IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 certification|Standard durability and safety tests.
An accredited installer|MCS (UK), NABCEP (US), Clean Energy Council (Australia).
A recycling scheme|PV Cycle membership or a national take-back programme.
EPEAT for solar or a low-carbon module declaration|Lower manufacturing footprint.
beware: Door-to-door 'free solar' offers|Read the lease terms.
Payback claims without your own usage data|Ask for a calculation based on your bills.

crit: Space and connection|Habitat loss and fragmentation are the main causes of wildlife decline. Climate change and pollution add to them.
look: Protected-area status and its rules|National park, nature reserve, marine protected area: stay on paths, follow seasonal closures.
Local conservation trusts and land trusts|Membership and volunteering directly fund protection.
Leave No Trace principles|Take everything out; keep dogs on leads near nesting birds.
Certified nature-positive tourism|Operators certified to a GSTC-recognised standard.
Citizen-science apps|iNaturalist and local recording schemes.
beware: Wildlife selfies, feeding and riding attractions|Usually harm the animals.
'Eco-lodge' without a certificate|Ask what it means.

crit: The fibre and the dye house|Growing or making the fibre, then dyeing and finishing it, are where most water, chemicals and carbon are used.
Who sewed it|Wages and safety in garment factories.
look: GOTS|Organic fibre with audited processing and labour standards.
OEKO-TEX Made in Green, bluesign|Chemical safety and responsible production.
Fairtrade Cotton, Fair Wear Foundation|Farmer prices and factory conditions.
Responsible Wool or Down Standard|For animal fibres.
A published factory list and repair service|Transparency and durability.
Second-hand, rental or swapping|Skips production altogether.
beware: 'Eco', 'conscious', 'green' collections|No standard behind the words.
'Recyclable' clothing|Under 1% of textiles are recycled into new clothes.
Very low prices|Someone else is paying.

crit: Raw materials|Extracting and processing materials causes about half of global emissions, so what it is made of and how long it lasts matter most.
look: A long guarantee and available spare parts|The simplest proxy for durability.
Recognised ecolabels|EU Ecolabel, Blue Angel, Nordic Swan, Cradle to Cradle Certified.
FSC for wood and paper, recycled content with a percentage|Verified material sourcing.
Energy label, if it plugs in|Compare kWh per year.
Repairability score or iFixit rating|Where available.
Second-hand, refurbished, borrowed or rented|Avoids new material.
beware: 'Eco-friendly', 'green', 'natural', 'planet-safe'|Vague terms that regulators increasingly treat as greenwashing unless backed by evidence.
'Carbon neutral' products|Usually offset-based.
Self-made logos that look like certifications|Search the logo: a real scheme has a public standard and an independent auditor.

crit: Unknown|Ripple could not identify this, so it cannot point to a hotspot.
look: A recognised, independently audited label|Real certifications publish their standard and name their auditor.
Durability, repairability and a guarantee|True for almost any made object.
beware: Vague green words with no evidence|'Eco', 'natural', 'sustainable', 'green'.
